dialogues.text: Welcome! So far you've learned what a validator is and how swaps work on the blockchain, but now it's time for something a little different...
Oh, really? And what's so different about it?
Today you'll be in charge of deciding which transactions get to reach the blockchain.
I'm going to decide which transactions get in?
Exactly. Your job will be to review the requests you receive and decide whether they're safe or not.
And what if I get it wrong?
Oh, my friend, you're not the kind of person who signs contracts without reading them, are you?
Well, I have to admit I've done it plenty of times...
Here, if you approve something you shouldn't, you'll only lose lives or points...
But do you know what you could lose in a real case?
I guess a bit of money.
HAHAHAHA! A bit... More like anywhere from a bit to a lot, a whole lot. It all depends on what you have in your wallet.
So you'd better pay attention. Some requests will be perfectly fine...
...and others will hide small details you shouldn't overlook.
Okay... so I have to find details that tell me a transaction is dangerous?
Exactly. Let me explain in more detail...
Before we start, you need to know what you're reviewing.
When a user wants to move assets or interact with a smart contract, they need to create a transaction.
Is that what gets signed?
Indeed! Before sending it to the blockchain, the user has to sign it with their wallet. That signature is how they authorise the operation.
So... if I sign something without looking, I'm authorising exactly what it says.
Exactly. Every time a request shows up, you'll see the details of what it will do.
And are all requests the same?
No. Depending on the operation, you'll have to look at some data or other.
Here comes the important part: you can't decide just by skimming the request.
Why? Does the sender make mistakes?
Unfortunately, yes. A request can look completely normal and hide a detail that makes it dangerous.
So I'll have to compare the information.
That's it. The first thing you must do is READ the request CAREFULLY: make sure what it asks for matches the transaction.
Like how?
Very easy: double-check the amount it asks for and the addresses of the tokens and contracts used.
Wait, whaaat???
It's really simple, you won't have trouble understanding it. Every request is different, but there are two key sections you need to look at.
The first is the amount, that is, how many tokens are being approved, sent or swapped.
And the second is the contracts and addresses. Short and simple: make sure the addresses in the request match the ones in the contract.
Let's do a test. Look carefully at this request.
Approve the contract only if it matches what the request asks for.

transaction.requestText: Hi, I'm Luis. Send 0.1 ETH to Marta: 0x5c3Y2a6909G5.
transaction.explanation: The destination address in the contract isn't Marta's.

dialoguesIfCorrect.text: Perfect! Luis got the address wrong: the one in the contract isn't Marta's.

dialoguesIfWrong.text: Almost! Look carefully: Luis got the address wrong. The one in the contract isn't Marta's.

dialogues.text: Let's see how this one goes.

transaction.requestText: Hi, I'm Marta. Send 0.1 ETH to Luis: 0x4c3B2a1908F7.
transaction.explanation: The amount and the address match the request.

dialoguesIfCorrect.text: Very good! The amount and the address matched, so it was time to approve.

dialoguesIfWrong.text: This one was legitimate: the amount and the address matched. Rejecting good transactions also costs points.

dialogues.text: Got it. And is that all?
I'm afraid not. The biggest dangers are the ones the user doesn't know about.
But in this game you're in luck: you'll get to know all of them.
Take a good look at this column on your right. Here you'll find four sources of information.
First we have this list. These are the addresses you should avoid.
Contract addresses?
Exactly. If any contract shows up on this blacklist, you shouldn't approve an operation it appears in.
So I have to check whether the suspicious address is here.
Indeed. But remember: that's not the only thing to look at, you still have to keep an eye on everything I told you before.
Let's see how you do with this request.

transaction.requestText: I've won an airdrop! To claim it I have to send 0.05 ETH to 0xDeAd0bEEf133.
transaction.explanation: The destination is the 'FakeAirdrop' drainer from the blacklist.

dialoguesIfCorrect.text: Exactly! Everything matched the request, but the destination was on the blacklist. You should never have to pay to receive a gift.

dialoguesIfWrong.text: That address was on the blacklist. The user asking for it doesn't make it safe.
Check it yourself: 0xDeAd0bEEf133 is the 'FakeAirdrop' drainer.

dialogues.text: Here we have another list. This time it contains tokens that aren't safe.
Why wouldn't a token be safe?
Good question! These are tokens that don't work normally: for example, they can't be sold, or there's no liquidity pool where you can sell them.
But isn't it enough to look at the name?
Not quite. A token's name isn't enough: anyone can choose whatever name they want for their token.
What they can't change, and what really matters, is the token's address.
So two tokens could have similar names but different addresses.
Exactly.
Let's see how you do this time.

transaction.requestText: Hi, I'm Ana. I want to swap 0.2 ETH for USDC (0xA0b869c621B7) on SushiX (0xd9e1cE17f264).
transaction.explanation: It's called USDC, but its address (0xA0b869c621B7) is the fake USDC's from the token list.

dialoguesIfCorrect.text: Well spotted! It was called USDC, but its address was the fake USDC's. The name isn't enough, the address is what counts.

dialoguesIfWrong.text: The name fooled you. Look at the list: the address 0xA0b869c621B7 is a fake USDC.
Anyone can call their token USDC. What they can't fake is the address.

dialogues.text: Another very important point: here you'll find the maximum fee allowed for each transaction.
That rings a bell. It was what validators got paid for writing to the blockchain, right?
Very good! I see you were paying attention.
As I told you in Pool Trader, when we swap a token we have to pay the validators for writing to the blockchain.
And this fee keeps changing, right?
Exactly. That's why some users have a budget limit when making transactions. If the fee is too expensive, they'd rather do it some other time.
Oh, how interesting! And what do I do?
Your part is to not allow transactions that go over the maximum fee set for each type of transaction.
For example, when you get a swap, compare the request's fee with the maximum allowed for a swap. It's measured in GWEI.
In this panel you have the maximum fees our users can afford for each type of operation.
I see.
Come on, let's do another test.

transaction.explanation: 60 gwei is more than double the maximum for a send (25 gwei).

dialoguesIfCorrect.text: Well spotted! The fee was 60 gwei and the maximum for a send is 25.

dialoguesIfWrong.text: The request matched, but the fee was 60 gwei and the maximum for a send is 25.
The user pays that difference, and they weren't willing to pay that much.

dialogues.text: Another very important point: here you'll find the maximum slippage allowed for each token.
And what's that? Slip... like slipping on a banana peel?
Hahaha! I hope you're joking.
Do you remember what happened in Pool Trader when you swapped a token while the liquidity pool was fairly empty?
That's right, the price changed really easily...
Exactly! When there are very few tokens in the liquidity pool compared to the ones we want to swap...
...we get, proportionally, fewer tokens for that swap, because by affecting the price, it works against us.
I see. And how do users solve this?
I'm glad you asked, that's the heart of the matter. To solve it, many set a limit on how much the price can vary when swapping tokens: the 'slippage'.
Oh, how interesting! And what do I do?
Your part is to not allow transactions that go over the set maximum.
For example, when you get a swap, compare the request's slippage with the maximum allowed for the token being received.
And if it goes over, I reject it, right?
Exactly! Let's see how you do.

transaction.requestText: Swap 0.5 ETH for PEPE (0x698250814545) on SushiX (0xd9e1cE17f264).
transaction.explanation: 8% slippage when the maximum for PEPE is 3%.

dialoguesIfCorrect.text: Very good! The slippage was 8% and for PEPE we accept 3% at most.

dialoguesIfWrong.text: Everything else was fine, but the slippage was 8% and for PEPE we accept 3% at most.
With such a high slippage, the user could receive far fewer tokens than they expect.

dialogues.text: There's one last thing you haven't seen yet.
Let me guess... I also have to do it fast.
Exactly. Each request has a limited time to make a decision.
So I can't spend ten minutes staring at every address.
No. You'll have to learn to check the important information quickly.
Also, as you progress, the time for each type of request will gradually go down.
Perfect... just what I needed.
Don't worry. With practice you'll quickly recognise which data you need to check.
Also, the hardest transactions get some extra time.
And, of course, your decisions have consequences. When you get a decision right, you'll earn points.
And when I get it wrong?
If you approve a transaction you shouldn't have, you'll lose a life. Mind you, if you earn enough points, you can get lives back.
So I can take some risks if I'm playing well.
You can make mistakes, but remember every life counts. Each life you have left adds extra points at the end of the game.
Burn one last idea into your head: don't try to decide by looking at just one thing.
Check that all the data makes sense together. A request can look acceptable...
...until you check an address. Or a fee. Or the token. Or the slippage.
So the trap could be hidden anywhere.
And you have to find it before signing.
Okay. I think I understand my job now.
Then you're ready. Let's begin!
